title: Living it close
hookLine: Jacob sleeps on a roadside stone and wakes: surely the LORD is in this place, and I knew it not
tomorrow: who was still beside him at the top of the mountain?

lines: HE WAKES ON THE SAME GROUND.
cards: The last day of something, a job, a season, a routine, and it turns out to be an ordinary Thursday. Nobody makes a speech. In Genesis, Jacob is on the run from his brother, alone.
The sun sets on a plain stretch of road. He takes one of the stones of that place for a pillow and lies down.
He dreams of a ladder set on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, angels going up and down on it, and God standing above it with a promise. Then he wakes up, on the same hard ground.

teach.h: SURELY THE LORD IS IN THIS PLACE.
teach.b: And he says: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." Then: "this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." Notice what place he means.
Not a temple. A roadside, with a rock for a pillow.
In the morning he sets that stone up as a pillar, pours oil on it, and names the spot Beth-el, house of God. The rabbis of the Talmud found one more thing in this night.

Genesis says Jacob lighted upon a certain place, and they read that as prayer, and credit Jacob with the evening prayer, maariv. So the man on the run, sleeping rough, becomes the father of praying at night.

That is the teaching Genesis hands down: God can be met in a place that looks like nothing, and the ordinary ground can turn out to be the gate. And that's what living it close means. Not waiting for the big moment.
The plain pickup, the evening review, the spice box, the one breath: this was it, the whole time.

how: Jews pray maariv, the evening prayer the Talmud ties to Jacob's night; readers of Genesis return to Jacob's waking at Beth-el as God met in an ordinary place, and people who borrow it look up from where they are.

o: a practice kept private from family and friends
the final exam at the end of a long course
practice brought home to plain days and places

p: his pillow, then a pillar with oil
on earth, its top reaching to heaven
the evening prayer tied to Jacob

s: in Genesis, Jacob sees the ladder at a temple
the popular picture. it's a roadside where he sleeps on a stone; only afterward does he call it the house of God.
the rabbis credit Jacob with the evening prayer
the Talmud reads his night at 'a certain place' as prayer.

games.q: your dad retires; his last day is emails and sheet cake in the break room, and he's deflated that it didn't feel like anything. what fits Jacob's waking?
o: the plain room can be the place: surely it was here, and he knew it not.
the meaning will come later, at a proper party with real speeches.
nothing holy happens at work; save that feeling for somewhere special.
games.why: Jacob's gate of heaven was a stone on an ordinary road. he set it up, poured oil on it, and named the place Beth-el.

practice: Let yourself lean back and rest, as if the ground beneath you were enough. When you're settled, lift your eyes: to the ceiling, the window, the sky. Stay with whatever is right there above you until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Living it close: practice brought home to plain days and places, the way Jacob found the gate of heaven by the road.

orig.note: Hebrew: Beth-el, house of God, the name Jacob gave the roadside place (Genesis 28:17-19).

carryVoice: Your line: this is it, the roadside and the stone, and I knew it not. Living it, done.

sources.ref: Genesis 28:10-19 (the stone for a pillow, the ladder, the pillar and oil, the name Beth-el)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 26b (Jacob instituted the evening prayer, from 'he lighted upon the place', Genesis 28:11)
